overview:
Padmapurana (more accurately Padmacharita or Padmacharitam) is a major Digambara Jain narrative scripture (prathamanuyoga) traditionally attributed to Acharya Ravishena (Ravishanacharya), usually dated to around the 7th–8th century CE. It belongs to the Jain Ramayana corpus and presents the life of Rama—known in Jain tradition as Padma, a Vasudeva and one of the 63 śalākā-puruṣas—from a distinctly Jain doctrinal and ethical perspective. The work is composed in Sanskrit kāvya style and is celebrated in Jain literary history for its poetic refinement, narrative breadth, and psychological insight into its characters.

Within the Digambara tradition, the text is often referred to as Padmapurana in modern printed editions and vernacular translations, but older colophons and scholarly studies emphasize that the more precise title is Padmacharita or Padmacharitam, meaning “the life-story (caritra) of Padmamuni (Rama).” The epic is regarded as one of the earliest extensive Jain retellings of the Ramayana story, standing alongside Vimalasuri’s Prakrit Paumacariyam and Swayambhu’s Apabhraṃśa Paumacariu. It forms part of a broader Jain purāṇic and caritra literature that reinterprets pan-Indian epic heroes—such as Rama and Kṛṣṇa—within the Jain cosmological and karmic framework.

Padmapurana narrates the genealogy of Ikṣvāku kings, the birth and upbringing of Padma (Rama), his exile, the abduction of Sītā, the campaigns against Rāvaṇa, and the eventual resolution of the conflict, but it does so while systematically reshaping the characters and events to align with Jain principles of ahiṃsā (non-violence), karma theory, and the ideal of spiritual progress. Rāvaṇa, for example, is not portrayed as a flesh-eating demon but as a powerful, complex ruler whose downfall is explained through karmic causality and ethical failings rather than inherent monstrosity. The text also integrates extensive sub-narratives about vidyādharas (celestial beings), auxiliary heroes such as Hanuman, and other legendary figures, creating a rich narrative universe that serves both as religious instruction and literary entertainment.

From a historical perspective, Padmacharita is considered one of the oldest surviving Digambara narrative works. Internal dating verses and comparative studies with other Jain purāṇas suggest a composition date around Vikrama Saṃvat 834, slightly earlier than Jinasena’s Harivaṃśapurāṇa (V.S. 840). Ravishena’s guru lineage is traced through Indraguru, Divākarayati, Arhanmuni, Lakṣmaṇasena, and finally Ravi (Ravishena), indicating his place within an early phase of Digambara scholastic and narrative activity before later sangha divisions became prominent. The work is frequently cited by subsequent Jain authors and is referenced in texts such as Kuvalayamālā and Harivaṃśapurāṇa, which helps situate it within the evolving Jain purāṇic tradition.

Doctrinally, Padmapurana functions as a vehicle for illustrating Jain views on right conduct (cāritra), the workings of karma, and the path to liberation, using the familiar Ramayana storyline as a framework. The narrative emphasizes vows, restraint, and the consequences of passion and violence, while also portraying the grandeur of royal life, warfare, and political intrigue in a way that remains compatible with Jain ethics. Listening to or studying the Ramayana in its Jain form is described in traditional prefaces as meritorious, capable of purifying karmic accumulations when approached with faith and understanding. Modern editions in Hindi, Gujarati, and other languages—often titled Padmapuran or Padmapuran Bhāṣā—have made the text accessible to lay audiences, reinforcing its role as a key bridge between classical Jain literature and contemporary devotional and study practices.

primary_sources.title: Padmacharita (Padmacharitam), commonly known as Padmapurana
primary_sources.author: Acharya Ravishena (Ravishanacharya)
primary_sources.original_text:
द्विशताभ्यधिके समासहस्त्रे समतीतेऽर्धचतुर्थवर्षयुक्ते ।
जिनभास्करवर्द्धमानसिद्धे चरितं पद्ममुनेरिदं निबद्धम् ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
dviśatābhyadhike samāsahasre samatīte 'rdha-caturtha-varṣa-yukte |
jinabhāskara-varddhamāna-siddhe caritaṃ padmamuner idaṃ nibaddham ||
primary_sources.translation: “When more than two hundred years and a thousand years had passed, together with three and a half years, after the attainment of liberation by the Jina-sun Vardhamāna, this life-story of Padmamuni was composed.”
primary_sources.notes: This colophon verse is used by traditional editors and modern scholars to date Padmacharita/Padmapurana relative to the nirvāṇa of Mahāvīra and the beginning of the Vikrama era. It underlies the commonly accepted dating of the work to around Vikrama Saṃvat 834 and supports the claim that Ravishena’s narrative predates Jinasena’s Harivaṃśapurāṇa. The verse appears in critical introductions to modern Sanskrit and vernacular editions published by Digambara institutions such as Manikchand Digambar Jain Granthamala Samiti and Bharatiya Jñānpīṭh, where it is cited as internal evidence for the text’s antiquity and authorship.

primary_sources.title: Opening invocations and narrative framing in Padmacharita
primary_sources.author: Acharya Ravishena (Ravishanacharya)
primary_sources.original_text: Traditional editions begin with maṅgalācaraṇa verses invoking Lord Mahāvīra and the Jinas, followed by statements that the pure character of Padmamuni (Rama) is being narrated to dispel misconceptions about him and other vidyādhara princes found in non-Jain Ramayana traditions.
primary_sources.transliteration: Exact Sanskrit wording varies by edition; typical colophons and introductions refer to the work as “śrī-padma-muneḥ caritam” and describe it as a prathamanuyoga (narrative) text composed by ācārya-ravīśena.
primary_sources.translation: Paraphrased: “Having bowed to the Jinas, I compose the life-story of Padmamuni, whose pure character has been obscured by the tales of foolish poets; may this narrative remove false views and lead the listener toward merit and right faith.”
primary_sources.notes: The precise Sanskrit of the opening verses differs slightly across manuscripts and printed editions, but the thematic elements are consistent: (1) an invocation of Mahāvīra and the Jinas, (2) identification of the work as the caritra of Padmamuni (Rama), and (3) a programmatic statement that the Jain Ramayana aims to correct distortions found in other tellings. Modern Gujarati and Hindi introductions to Padmapurana (often titled Śrī Padma Purāṇa or Śrī Rāmcarit) explicitly highlight this corrective intention and link it to questions posed to Mahāvīra about Rāvaṇa and his followers in earlier Jain texts.

primary_sources.title: Padmapuran Bhāṣā (vernacular Hindi rendition of Padmacharita/Padmapurana)
primary_sources.author: Based on Acharya Ravishena; vernacular adaptation by Digambar Jain Granth Pracharak Pustakalay
primary_sources.original_text: The Hindi prose and verse adaptation presents the narrative of Padma (Rama), Sītā, Rāvaṇa, Hanuman, and related figures, embedding Jain doctrinal explanations of karma, ahiṃsā, and the status of Tirthankaras and śalākā-puruṣas. It begins with a maṅgalācaraṇa to Mahāvīra and proceeds through large mahā-adhikāras (great chapters).
primary_sources.transliteration: Not applicable; the text is primarily in modern Hindi, occasionally citing Sanskrit ślokas from the original Padmacharita.
primary_sources.translation: Representative English paraphrase: “In the auspicious presence of Lord Mahāvīra’s teaching assembly, the story of Padma, the illustrious Vasudeva, is told—how, bound by karma yet guided by dharma, he passes through joy and sorrow, conflict and peace, so that beings may understand the fruits of their own actions and turn toward the path of liberation.”
primary_sources.notes: Padmapuran Bhāṣā is a widely circulated Hindi adaptation used in lay study circles and community education. It follows Ravishena’s structure while explaining difficult points in accessible language, often adding explicit doctrinal commentary on non-violence, vows, and karmic consequences. Because it is a secondary vernacular work, it is treated as a Tier D community-education source rather than a primary canonical text, but it plays an important role in transmitting the content of Padmacharita to contemporary audiences.

primary_sources.title: Gujarati Padma Purana (Śrī Rāmcarit) based on Ravishena’s Padmacharita
primary_sources.author: Acharya Ravishena (source text); Gujarati translation by Śrī Digambar Jain Svādhyāy Mandir Trust
primary_sources.original_text: The Gujarati edition reproduces selected Sanskrit verses from Padmacharita and provides Gujarati prose explanations. It emphasizes that Rama’s story, when heard in its Jain form, destroys sins and clarifies the true character of Rama and Rāvaṇa, contrasting it with the Valmiki Ramayana.
primary_sources.transliteration: Sanskrit verses are transliterated in Devanagari; the Gujarati commentary explains terms like Vasudeva, śalākā-puruṣa, and prathamanuyoga.
primary_sources.translation: Representative English paraphrase: “The name of Rama is renowned throughout Bhāratavarṣa, yet his true character is known only through the teachings of the Jina. In this Padma Purana, the life of Padma is narrated according to Jain doctrine, so that misconceptions born of other Ramayanas may be removed and right understanding may arise.”
primary_sources.notes: This Gujarati Padma Purana is an important bridge text for Gujarati-speaking Digambara communities. Its introduction explicitly situates Ravishena’s work among other Jain Ramayanas (such as Vimalasuri’s Paumacariyam and Hemacandra’s Triṣaṣṭi-śalākā-puruṣa-caritra) and discusses its relationship to the Valmiki Ramayana. While not itself a primary Sanskrit composition, it preserves and interprets key themes of Padmacharita and is frequently cited in modern Jain scholarship and community study materials.

misconceptions.myth: Padmapurana is the same text as the Hindu Padma Purana and belongs to the Brahmanical Purāṇa corpus.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain usage, Padmapurana (more precisely Padmacharita/Padmacharitam) is a distinct Digambara Jain narrative work attributed to Acharya Ravishena. It is a Jain Ramayana that reinterprets the life of Rama (Padma) according to Jain doctrine and is not part of the Hindu Padma Purana or the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas of the Brahmanical tradition. The similarity of names often leads to confusion, but the contents, language, and sectarian context are different.

misconceptions.myth: The proper title of the work is only Padmapurana, and Padmacharita is a later or secondary name.
misconceptions.reality: Manuscript colophons and early references in Jain literature identify the work as Padmacharita or Padmacharitam, meaning “the life-story of Padmamuni.” The designation Padmapurana became common in later printed editions and vernacular adaptations, but traditional scholarship emphasizes that Padmacharita is the more accurate original title. Both names are used in modern Jain circles, yet recognizing Padmacharita helps situate the text correctly within the Jain caritra genre.

misconceptions.myth: Jain Padmapurana portrays Rāvaṇa and his followers as flesh-eating, blood-drinking demons in the same way as some non-Jain Ramayana traditions.
misconceptions.reality: Jain narrative texts, including Padmacharita/Padmapurana, explicitly reject the depiction of Rāvaṇa and related figures as inherently demonic or cannibalistic. Instead, they present Rāvaṇa as a powerful but ethically flawed ruler whose actions are explained through karma and moral choices. The text criticizes “foolish poets” for distorting the character of vidyādhara princes and uses the Ramayana story to illustrate Jain principles of non-violence, restraint, and karmic retribution rather than to demonize entire groups of beings.

misconceptions.myth: Padmapurana is a purely mythological story with no doctrinal or ethical significance for Jain practice.
misconceptions.reality: Although Padmacharita/Padmapurana is a narrative epic, it is structured as prathamanuyoga literature, intended to convey Jain doctrine through stories. It illustrates the workings of karma, the importance of vows and right conduct, and the consequences of passion, violence, and attachment. Traditional prefaces and modern commentaries emphasize that listening to or studying the Jain Ramayana in this form is meritorious and can support right faith and ethical living, making the text both literary and spiritually instructive.

misconceptions.myth: Padmapurana is a late, derivative work with little historical importance in Jain literature.
misconceptions.reality: Internal dating verses and references in other Jain texts indicate that Padmacharita/Padmapurana is one of the earliest extensive Digambara narrative works, likely composed in the 7th–8th century CE and slightly predating Jinasena’s Harivaṃśapurāṇa. It is cited by later authors and is recognized in modern scholarship as a foundational Jain Ramayana, alongside earlier Prakrit and Apabhraṃśa versions. Its age, influence, and literary quality give it significant historical importance within the Jain purāṇic and caritra tradition.
